extracted.intended_audience: educated British public, politicians, and readers of political/polemical essays concerned with the French Revolution
extracted.subtask_description: A conservative political-polemical essay (late 18th century) critiquing the French Revolution's violence, institutions, and social consequences; arguing for the civilizing role of manners, religion, and traditional authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of triumphalizing mob violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Triumphal processions celebrating the overthrow and humiliation of monarchs (dragging a king 'in submissive triumph') are unmanly, irreligious, and profane; sacred expressions (e.g. 'Nunc dimittis') must not be applied to scenes of massacre and atrocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such spectacles shock moral taste, resemble savage processions rather than civilized triumphs, and should not be consecrated by thanksgiving or religious language. Avoid celebrating popular violence as a moral good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative assemblies must be free from coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: An assembly surrounded by a foreign/armed force, subject to terror (bayonet, lamp-post, torch), and in the presence of an intimidating mob cannot deliberate impartially; their votes under such necessity lack genuine liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative bodies must possess independence of residence, command, and authority; laws and measures decided under coercion are illegitimate and mere farce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public measures must not be formed by clubs or academies promoting violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Clubs and academies set up as seminaries for revolutionary clubs deform public measures into daring, violent, and perfidious counsels; audacity is mistaken for genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid institutionalizing decision-making through unruly popular clubs; deliberation should be insulated from the incentives that valorize violence and spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity and compassion are essential civic virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanity, compassion, and tenderness towards individuals should not be ridiculed as superstition or ignorance; ridiculing these sentiments is an intellectual and moral error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy and discourse should preserve sympathy for individuals; scorning tenderness leads to cruelty and the erosion of civilized norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty must not be equated solely with property interest or material calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating liberty purely as a matter of property or private interest (mechanic philosophy) banishes the affections that sustain social institutions and makes laws depend only on terrors or private calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and political systems require attachments, manners, and affections beyond narrow economic self-interest to function well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative bodies should present the dignity and physiognomy of a grave assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: An assembly that resembles comedians before a riotous audience and lacks color or aspect of a grave legislative body undermines legitimacy and cannot construct durable institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain decorum, sober procedure, and institutional dignity in representative bodies to foster public confidence and effective lawmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: History will judge atrocities despite flattery or amnesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to console or flatter victims (or to drug memory with 'amnesty' clothed in scorn) do not erase the record; history preserves a durable censure of such proceedings (e.g., the October 6th atrocities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on rhetorical consolation or pardon to obscure crimes; acknowledge and record abuses honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must be supported by manners, religion, and public affections, not only by terror
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilization in Europe has depended on the combined principles of the spirit of a gentleman and the spirit of religion; when manners and opinions perish, laws resting only on terrors become unstable and inhuman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate manners, education, religion, and public affections as supplements and correctives to law; legal systems should aspire to be 'lovely' as well as just (Non satis est pulchra esse poemata, dulcia sunto).

rubrics_metrics.name: A nation's manners make it lovable and sustain patriotic attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be a system of manners in every nation which makes the country lovable and thereby fosters love and attachment to the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should preserve social mores and institutions that render the country attractive to its citizens; love of country is cultivated through character and manners, not merely by statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destruction of ancient principles yields loss of moral compass and worse forms of tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: When ancient opinions and rules of life are removed, society loses its compass and power survives by more brutal arts (preventive murder, confiscation); plots and assassinations will be anticipated by preventive crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware radical overthrow of long-standing principles; institutional change should consider the unintended substitution of worse mechanisms of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chivalrous spirit and religion are pillars of learning and civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The nobility (spirit of a gentleman) and the clergy (spirit of religion) historically kept learning and manners alive; their union produced many civilizing benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect traditional institutions that sustain education, manners, and mutual esteem; do not debauch learning with unchecked ambition that severs it from its civilizing patrons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutions that subvert institutions will use similar subversive arts to hold power
rubrics_metrics.description: The usurpation that destroys ancient institutions to subvert them will subsequently hold power by arts similar to those it used to acquire it (plots, assassination, confiscation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the means of acquisition of power shape the means of its maintenance; revolutionary methods tend to perpetuate further subversion and brutality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not relativize regicide, parricide, or sacrilege as ordinary homicide
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating the murder of kings, bishops, or fathers as mere common homicide (and more pardonable if politically useful) is a dangerous moral relativism that corrupts jurisprudence and moral judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain distinctions in moral and legal treatment of politically and socially consequential crimes; avoid normalizing political murders by utilitarian calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public spectacles of humiliation and savage display are signs of moral decay
rubrics_metrics.description: Parading captives, mounting severed heads, and applauding atrocities (including women's ferocious participation) are not civilized triumphs but evidences of barbarism and the collapse of honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condemn and avoid public displays that degrade persons into trophies; civilized nations should preserve honourable conduct even amid conflict.
